title: Allegory allowed for the gods but not for Moses
source_text: Ἐν δὲ τοῖς ἑξῆς κατηγορῶν τῆς Μω(??)σέως ἱστορίας αἰτιᾶται τοὺς τροπολογοῦντας καὶ ἀλληγοροῦντας αὐτήν. ἦν δ᾿ ἂν εἰπεῖν πρὸς τὸν γενναιότατον καὶ ἀληθῆ λόγον ἐπιγράψαντα τὸ ἑαυτοῦ βιβλίον. τί δήποτε. ὦ οὗτος. θεοὺς μὲν τηλικαύταις περιπίπτοντας συμφοραῖς. ὁποίας ἀναγράφουσιν οἱ σοφοί σου ποιηταὶ καὶ φιλόσοφοι, καὶ ἐναγέσι μίξεσι χρωμένους καὶ κατὰ τῶν πατέρων στρατευομένους καὶ τὰ αἰδοῖα αὐτῶν ἀποτέμνοντας σεμνολογεῖς ἀναγεγράφθαι τὰ τηλικαῦτα τετολμηκέναι καὶ πεποιηκέναι καὶ πεπονθέναι· ὅταν δὲ Μω(??)σῆς μὴ περὶ θεοῦ τοιαῦτα λέγῃ ἀλλὰ μηδ᾿ ἀγγέλων ἁγίων περὶ δὲ ἀνθρώπων πολλῷ ἐλάττονα (οὐδεὶς γὰρ παρ᾿ αὐτῷ ἐτόλμησεν ὅσα Κρόνος κατὰ τοῦ Οὐρανοῦ οὐδ᾿ ὅσα Ζεὺς κατὰ τοῦ πατρὸς, οὐδ᾿ ὅτι τῇ ἑαυτοῦ θυγατρὶ ὁ „πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε“ συνελήλυθεν), πλανᾶν νομίζετε ἠπατημένους τοὺς νενομοθετημένους ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ; δοκεῖ δὲ μοι καὶ παραπλήσιόν τι Κέλσος ποιεῖν τῷ Πλατωνικῷ Θρασυμάχῳ, μὴ ἐπιτρέποντι ὡς βούλεται ἀποκρίνασθαι περὶ τῆς δικαιοσύνης Σωκράτει ἀλλὰ λέγοντι· ὅρα μὴ τὸ συμφέρον εἴπῃς εἶναι τὸ δίκαιον μηδὲ τὸ δέον μηδ᾿ ἄλλο τι τῶν παραπλησίων. καὶ γὰρ οὗτος κατηγορήσας, ὡς οἴεται. τῶν παρὰ Μωϋσεῖ ἱστοριῶν καὶ μεμψάμενος τοῖς ἀλληγοροῦσι μετὰ τοῦ καὶ ἔπαινόν τινα περὶ αὐτῶν λέγειν, ὅτι εἰσὶν οἱ ἐπιεικέστεροι. οἱονεὶ κωλύεται κατηγορήσας, ὡς βούλεται, ἀπολογεῖσθαι τοὺς δυναμένους. ὡς πέφυκεν ἔχειν τὰ πράγματα.
pass_a_gloss: In the following, accusing (κατηγορέω) the history (ἱστορία) of Moses, he blames (αἰτιάομαι) those who interpret it figuratively (τροπολογέω) and allegorise (ἀλληγορέω) it. One could say to the most noble (γενναιότατος) one who entitled (ἐπιγράφω) his own book True Doctrine (ἀληθὴς λόγος): Why ever, O you (ὦ οὗτος), do you speak solemnly (σεμνολογέω) of its having been written that gods, falling into (περιπίπτω) such great calamities (συμφορά) as your wise poets and philosophers record, and using accursed (ἐναγής) minglings/unions (μίξις) and campaigning (στρατεύομαι) against their fathers and cutting off (ἀποτέμνω) their genitals (αἰδοῖα), dared (τολμάω) and did and suffered (πάσχω) such things; but when Moses says such things not about God, nor even about holy angels, but about men much lesser things (for no one in him dared what Cronus against Uranus, nor what Zeus against his father, nor that the 'father of men and gods' had intercourse (συνέρχομαι) with his own daughter), you (pl.) think that he leads astray (πλανάω), deceived (ἀπατάω, pf. pass. ptc.), those legislated (νομοθετέω) by him? And it seems to me that Celsus does something similar to the Platonic Thrasymachus, not permitting (ἐπιτρέπω) Socrates to answer as he wishes about justice (δικαιοσύνη) but saying: See you do not say the just (τὸ δίκαιον) is the advantageous (τὸ συμφέρον) nor the needful (τὸ δέον) nor anything else of the like. For this man too, having accused, as he thinks (οἴομαι), the histories in Moses and having blamed (μέμφομαι) those who allegorise, along with also saying some praise (ἔπαινος) about them, that they are the more reasonable (ἐπιεικέστεροι), as it were (οἱονεί) prevents (κωλύω), having accused as he wishes, those who are able (δύναμαι) from defending (ἀπολογέομαι) as the matters naturally are (ὡς πέφυκεν ἔχειν τὰ πράγματα).
pass_b_english: In what follows, while accusing the history written by Moses, he finds fault with those who interpret it figuratively and allegorically. One might say to this most noble man, who gave his own book the title True Doctrine: “Why on earth, sir, do you speak with reverence of the records that gods fell into such great calamities as your wise poets and philosophers describe, that they engaged in abominable unions, made war on their fathers and castrated them, and that they dared, did and suffered such things? And yet when Moses says nothing of the kind about God, nor even about holy angels, but tells far lesser things about men (for no one in his writings dared what Cronus did against Uranus, nor what Zeus did against his father, nor did ‘the father of men and gods’ (Homer, Iliad 1.544) lie with his own daughter), do you people think that he leads astray those who received laws from him, and that they have been deceived?”

It seems to me that Celsus is doing something like Plato’s Thrasymachus, who would not allow Socrates to answer as he wished about justice, but said: “See that you do not say that the just is the advantageous, or what is needful, or anything else of that sort” (Plato, Republic 336c–d). For Celsus too, having accused (as he supposes) the histories in Moses, and having blamed those who allegorize them while also giving them some praise, saying they are “the more reasonable,” as it were prevents those who are able from making a defence that answers to the true nature of the matters, once he has made his accusations as he pleases.

choices.choice: Staged Greek shows '(??)' inside Μωϋσῆς and its cases (Μω(??)υσῆς, Μω(??)σέως): an encoding artefact for the diaeresis, no textual effect. Origen's imagined address moves from singular (σεμνολογεῖς) to plural (νομίζετε); the plural is rendered 'you people'. 'πλανᾶν νομίζετε ἠπατημένους τοὺς νενομοθετημένους ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ': the perfect participle ἠπατημένους agrees with the lawgiven people (they are the deceived), so rendered 'he leads astray those who received laws from him, and that they have been deceived'. 'ὁ πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε' is a Homeric formula (first at Iliad 1.544, often after); the union of Zeus with his daughter is the Orphic story of Zeus and Persephone (not cited inline). Cronus castrating Uranus and Zeus warring on Cronus follow Hesiod's Theogony (not cited inline; general mythic reference). Thrasymachus's demand is Plato, Republic 336c–d; Origen gives a shortened paraphrase, rendered from Origen's wording. 'οἱ ἐπιεικέστεροι' is Celsus's praise of the allegorizers, so it is set in quotation marks (Celsus means the more reasonable of the Jewish and Christian interpreters; nothing is added in the English). 'True Doctrine' is the title of Celsus's book (ἀληθὴς λόγος); 'most noble' is ironic. No Scripture quoted.
τί δήποτε, ὦ οὗτος: 'Why, my good sir' -> 'Why on earth, sir' (ὦ οὗτος is brusque, not polite; matches 'sir' in 1.18)
τὰ αἰδοῖα αὐτῶν ἀποτέμνοντας: 'cut off their genitals' -> 'castrated them' (removes ambiguity: the fathers' genitals)

πλανᾶν νομίζετε ἠπατημένους τοὺς νενομοθετημένους: 'he deceived and led astray' (past tense, active deceiving added) -> 'he leads astray those who received laws from him, and that they have been deceived' (present infinitive kept; perfect passive participle kept on the people)

last sentence restructured: 'from defending the histories as the facts naturally require' -> 'from making a defence that answers to the true nature of the matters' (object 'the histories' was supplied, not in the Greek; ὡς πέφυκεν ἔχειν τὰ πράγματα rendered closer)
checked Iliad 1.544 (πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε) and Republic 336c–d (τὸ δέον, τὸ συμφέρον): correct
